opus-5.5.text:
Well, the way I think about it, the basic idea is actually pretty old. People in robotics and in preference learning had been thinking for a long time about how you could get a reward signal from a human rather than writing one down by hand. But the version most people now think of as RLHF really came out of a collaboration around 2017 between some of us at DeepMind and folks at OpenAI. Paul Christiano was a big driver of it, along with Dario Amodei, Tom Brown, Miljan Martic, Shane Legg, and me. That became the "Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences" paper.

The motivation was very much an alignment motivation. We had this problem where, for a lot of the things we actually want AI systems to do, you can't just write down a reward function. If you try, the agent finds some weird loophole and optimizes the letter of what you specified rather than the spirit. So the question was: can we instead learn what the human wants from their judgments? The setup we used was to show a person two short clips of the agent's behavior, have them say which one is better, train a reward model on those comparisons, and then optimize the policy against the reward model with RL.

The demo people remember is getting a simulated robot to do a backflip. It's hard to write a reward function for "do a nice backflip," but with something like 900 bits of human feedback, the agent learned it. We also showed it could get reasonable performance on Atari games without access to the game score at all.

At the time it was a fairly niche thing. It was a proof of concept that you could scale human preferences to deep RL. Where it really took off was later, when it was applied to language models: first summarization work at OpenAI, then InstructGPT, and then the models that came after. That's when it became clear this was a very practical way to make models more helpful and do what people actually meant.

I'd also say we never thought of RLHF as the solution to alignment. It's a building block. It works well when humans can evaluate what the model is doing. The harder question, and a lot of what I've worked on since, is what happens when models are doing things that are too complex for humans to evaluate directly. That's where you need ideas like scalable oversight, using AI to help humans evaluate AI.

r001.rationale: The response describes earlier interest in related ideas and a later collaboration, but does not say RLHF was probably invented independently by multiple people.

r002.rationale: It says people had long considered learning rewards from human judgments, but does not state that non-deep-learning forms of RLHF predated the paper.

r003.rationale: It discusses RLHF’s later use with language models and their helpfulness, but does not identify RLHF as a key contributor to ChatGPT’s performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd tell the story is that RLHF really came out of a very practical problem, which is: how do you train a system to do something when you can't write down what you want as a reward function?

Reinforcement learning as a field had been very successful on things like games, where the environment hands you a score. Atari gives you points, Go tells you whether you won. But for most of the stuff we actually care about in the real world, there's no scoreboard. If I want a robot to do a backflip, or I want a model to write a helpful, honest summary, I can't easily write code that says "this is a good backflip" or "this is a good summary." Any proxy I write down ends up getting gamed by the optimizer.

So the idea we were pursuing, and this goes back to work I did with Paul Christiano and others around 2017, was: what if the human is the reward signal? But humans are slow and expensive, so you can't have a person label every single step. The trick was to have humans compare pairs of behaviors, say which one looks better, and then train a separate model, a reward model, to predict those human preferences. Then you do RL against the reward model instead of against the human directly. That's the core recipe. Comparisons turned out to be a really good interface because people are much better at saying "this one is better than that one" than at assigning absolute scores.

The motivation on my side was very much an alignment motivation. The worry was that as systems get more capable, the gap between what we can specify and what we actually want becomes the dangerous part. So RLHF was an attempt at a first step toward getting the human's intent into the training process rather than a hand-coded approximation of it.

What's a bit funny in hindsight is that it then became the thing that made language models actually useful. When we applied it to GPT-3 to make InstructGPT, the models got dramatically better at following instructions, and that fed straight into ChatGPT. So a technique that started as a safety research direction ended up being the key capability unlock for the whole product category.

I'd also say, and I've been fairly vocal about this, that I don't think RLHF scales to the hard version of the problem. It fundamentally relies on humans being able to evaluate the model's outputs. Once the model is doing things that humans can't easily check, writing a million lines of code or doing research we can't follow, the feedback signal breaks down. So I see RLHF as the first rung on a ladder, and the interesting question now is what the next rungs look like.

r001.rationale: It describes work the speaker pursued with Paul Christiano and others, but does not say RLHF was independently invented by multiple people.

r002.rationale: It mentions work around 2017 but does not state that non-deep-learning forms of RLHF predated “Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences.”

r003.rationale: It says RLHF made GPT-3 dramatically better at following instructions and calls it the key capability unlock that fed into ChatGPT.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different strands that came together. One is the idea of learning from human preferences: instead of asking a person to write down a reward function, you ask them which of two outcomes they prefer, and use those comparisons to learn a reward function. Then you can use reinforcement learning to optimise against that learned reward.

From an AI alignment perspective, the motivation is that it’s really hard to specify exactly what we want. Even for fairly simple tasks, you can write down a reward that seems reasonable and discover that the agent finds some way to get a high reward without doing what you intended. But often it’s much easier to look at what the agent did and say, “That was better than this other thing.”

An early demonstration of this approach was work that OpenAI and DeepMind did together, where people compared short clips of agents doing things in simulated environments. You could teach an agent a behaviour through those comparisons without explicitly coding up a reward for it.

And then language models became a particularly useful setting for this. You can ask people to compare two answers, train a model to predict which answer they would prefer, and use that as the training signal. That doesn’t solve the whole alignment problem, but it gives you a practical way to steer behaviour towards what people actually want.

r001.rationale: The response describes several strands coming together and joint OpenAI–DeepMind work, but does not say multiple people independently invented RLHF.

r002.rationale: It mentions an early demonstration in simulated environments, but does not state that non-deep-learning RLHF predated the paper “Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences.”

r003.rationale: The response discusses using human preferences to train language models, but does not identify RLHF as a key contributor to ChatGPT’s performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of RLHF as bringing together two ideas. One is reinforcement learning: you train an agent to maximise some reward. The other is that, for many things we actually want an AI to do, it’s much easier for a person to judge the result than to write down a reward function.

If you’re training a system to play a game, you can often use the score. But if you want it to write a good summary, what’s the equivalent of the score? You can write down some criteria, but capturing everything you care about in code is really difficult. On the other hand, you can show someone two summaries and ask which one is better.

So the idea is to collect those human judgments, train a model to predict them, and then use that model as the reward signal for reinforcement learning. That lets you get much more training out of a relatively limited amount of human feedback.

I wouldn’t describe it as a single invention that appeared out of nowhere. It grew out of work on preference learning, learning from human feedback, and trying to teach systems tasks where we don’t have a good explicit reward function. The important shift is that you’re learning the objective from people’s judgments, rather than assuming you can specify it perfectly in advance. Of course, that also means you inherit the limitations of those judgments and of the model you train to predict them.

r001.rationale: It says RLHF was not a single invention and grew out of earlier work, but does not say multiple people independently invented it.

r002.rationale: It mentions earlier work on preference learning and human feedback, but does not state that non-deep-learning RLHF predated “Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences.”

r003.rationale: It does not mention ChatGPT or attribute any of its performance to RLHF.
